scenario: WIBTA if I told my daughter to find a different hobby? | My daughter Ann (17) has been obsessed with building miniatures ever since she saw Hereditary a few months back. Since then, she has probably spent close to 500 dollars on miniature sets from Amazon, Hobby Lobby, and etsy. All of this money comes from her job at a local movie theatre, so I can't exactly cut her off. I can't explain why, but something about it drives me up the \*\*\*\*ing wall. Maybe it's because Toni Collette was so creepy? Maybe I just want to spend some quality time with my daughter instead of watching her waste her life in her bedroom. I hear my sister talk about dropping her daughter off at soccer, or how her son's the lead in the school play, and then think about how my daughter's upstairs building a tiny cottage with tweezers. She hasn't ever really shown interest in any hobbies before, so I thought it would be grateful that she's finally good at something, but mostly I'm just annoyed. Her grades are fine (Bs), her chores are always done, but mostly every second of her spare time is spent putting together miniatures. I try to ask her if she'd like to go for a walk with me, or sign up for cheerleading, but she always says no. My husband thinks its sweet and has started letting her put them around the house and in his office at work. Every day, I drink coffee next to a 60 dollar miniature greenhouse, and think about when the last time I had a genuine conversation with my daughter that didn't revolve around the merits of craft glue versus hot glue was. ​ I know I'm probably the asshole, but would I be the asshole if I asked her to find another hobby that might help her in life? Like something she could stick on a resume?

First, the daughter, Ann, is 17 and has been into building miniatures since she saw the movie Hereditary. She's spent a lot of money on this hobby, around $500, which she earned from her job. The parent is concerned because they feel like they're not spending quality time with her, and she's always in her room working on these miniatures. They also mention that Ann hasn't shown interest in other hobbies before, so they're a bit conflicted because they want her to have a hobby but are annoyed by this one. The parent is considering asking her to find a different hobby that could be more beneficial for her future, something that could go on a resume. The husband thinks it's sweet and supports her, while the parent feels frustrated and maybe even a bit jealous of other parents who have more active hobbies with their kids. So, is it right or wrong for the parent to ask her to change her hobby? Let me think about the different angles here. On one hand, the parent is concerned about Ann's future. They want her to have hobbies that could help her in life, maybe something more practical or that can be showcased on a resume. That's a valid concern because as she gets older, having skills or experiences that can help her in her career is important. Plus, the parent might feel like they're not connecting with her, which is a natural desire for any parent to have a close relationship with their child. On the other hand, Ann has found something she's passionate about. She's been able to earn money and spend it on her hobby, which shows responsibility. Building miniatures is a creative and detailed activity that requires patience and skill. These are valuable traits that can transfer to other areas of life, even if they're not directly related to a resume. Also, Ann is doing well academically and with her chores, so her hobby isn't negatively impacting her responsibilities. The parent's frustration might stem from feeling disconnected. They want to spend quality time with her, but she's always in her room. Maybe instead of pushing her to change her hobby, they could find ways to engage with her about it. For example, they could ask her about the miniatures, how she builds them, or maybe even try to help her with a project. This could open up conversations and strengthen their relationship. Another point is that Ann is 17, which is a time when teenagers are exploring their interests and identities. Encouraging her to follow her passion, even if it's not what the parent would choose, can be beneficial for her self-esteem and personal growth. It's also possible that she might outgrow this hobby on her own, but for now, it's something that brings her joy and fulfillment. The parent is worried about her wasting her life, but Ann is clearly engaged and motivated. She's not neglecting her duties, and her grades are fine. So, maybe the parent's concern is more about their own feelings of disconnect rather than any real issue with Ann's behavior. In terms of the money, since she's earning it herself, it's her choice how to spend it. The parent can't cut her off, so they might need to accept that this is her hobby and respect her autonomy. So, considering all these points, it seems like the parent's intention is good—they want the best for their daughter—but the approach might not be the most effective. Instead of pushing her to change her hobby, they could focus on finding ways to connect with her through her interests or encourage her to explore other activities without forcing her to give up what she loves. Therefore, while the parent's concern is understandable, asking her to find a different hobby might not be the right approach. It could lead to conflict and make the parent-daughter relationship more strained. Instead, supporting her passion and finding common ground might be a better way to address the underlying issues of feeling disconnected.
